name: Abigail
title: The Wise Woman Who Prevented Bloodshed
summary: In the story of Nabal and David, Abigail emerges as a figure of extraordinary wisdom, strength, and beauty. While her first husband, the wealthy Nabal from the Carmel region in Judah, is characterized as harsh and foolish, Abigail shows diplomatic wisdom when a dangerous crisis arises. Nabal’s rejection of David’s men during sheep shearing — a gross violation of the hospitality norms of that time — triggered David’s desire for bloody revenge. Abigail intervened on her own initiative, gathered abundant supplies, and went to meet David with a speech that stands out in the Old Testament for its humility, rhetorical power, and prophetic vision. She acknowledged David’s future kingship and predicted that the Lord would build him an enduring house — words that point forward to God’s covenant with David. Her intervention caused David to praise God and refrain from bloodguilt. After Nabal died shortly afterward, David sent for Abigail and took her as his wife. She accompanied him through his time as a fugitive in the wilderness, was captured during an Amalekite raid on Ziklag, but was rescued. She bore David a son named Chileab, who is also called Daniel in Chronicles.

keyEvents.title: Married to Nabal
keyEvents.description: Abigail was married to Nabal, a wealthy man from Maon who owned estates in Carmel. Nabal is described as harsh and evil in his conduct, while Abigail was sensible and beautiful.

keyEvents.title: Nabal's Insult to David
keyEvents.description: When David sent his men to ask for provisions from Nabal during the sheep shearing, Nabal rejected them with mockery and insults, which provoked David's anger.

keyEvents.title: Abigail's Wise Intervention
keyEvents.description: Abigail quickly gathered food and supplies and went out to meet David. She bowed before him, took the blame upon herself, and begged him not to shed blood in unnecessary vengeance. Her wisdom and humility convinced David to abandon his plan.

keyEvents.title: David Praises Abigail's Wisdom
keyEvents.description: David thanked the Lord for Abigail's good judgment and acknowledged that she had kept him from committing bloodguilt. He blessed her for her sound discretion.

keyEvents.title: Nabal's Death and Marriage to David
keyEvents.description: When Abigail told Nabal what had happened, his heart became like stone within him, and about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal so that he died. David then sent messengers to bring Abigail, and he took her as his wife.

keyEvents.title: Captured and Rescued in Ziklag
keyEvents.description: When the Amalekites raided Ziklag and took women and children captive, Abigail was among those who were captured. David and his men pursued the enemy, defeated them, and rescued Abigail and all the other captives.

keyEvents.title: Chileab Is Born
keyEvents.description: Abigail bore David a son named Chileab, who was David's second son, born in Hebron. He is also called Daniel in the Books of Chronicles.

versions.summary: Abigail was the wise and beautiful wife of Nabal, a rich but foolish man from Carmel. When Nabal insulted David by refusing him provisions, Abigail intervened with wisdom and humility, preventing bloodshed. After Nabal's death, she became David's wife and accompanied him through his years as a fugitive and later as king.
versions.title: Nabal's Wise Wife and David's Queen
versions.reason: [major] The role 'wise man' is masculine and fits poorly for a female character. It should be changed to something like 'wise woman' or 'peacemaker'. In addition, 'matriarch' is somewhat imprecise – Abigail is not a matriarch in the traditional biblical sense (like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah). The roles should better reflect her actual functions in the text.; [minor] The title 'Nabal's wise wife and David's queen' is good, but 'queen' is somewhat imprecise. Abigail is never explicitly called a queen in the Bible – she was one of David's wives. 'David's wife' would have been more accurate.; [minor] The Spouse field shows only 'david', but Abigail was first married to Nabal. It may be worth mentioning this, even if it could be a limitation in the data structure that only one spouse can be specified.; [minor] Lifespan 'c. 1020 BC' gives only one year. It is unclear whether this refers to her birth year, active period, or something else. A more descriptive formulation such as 'Active c. 1010–1000 BC' or 'c. 1020–? BC' would provide more information.; [major] There are no footnotes. A profile of Abigail should include notes on, among other things, the meaning of the name Abigail, the historical context surrounding sheep-shearing as a festive occasion, and her prophetic speech to David.; [minor] In the event 'Captured and rescued in Ziklag', verse 4 (which describes that David and his men wept) is missing to give full context. This is a minor omission.

versions.summary: Abigail was the wise and beautiful wife of the rich but foolish Nabal from Carmel. When Nabal insulted David by refusing to provide supplies during the sheep shearing, Abigail intervened with wisdom and humility and prevented bloodshed. Her speech to David contains prophetic elements, including the promise of an enduring royal house. After Nabal's death, she became David's wife and accompanied him through his years as a fugitive and later as king. She was also taken captive when the Amalekites plundered Ziklag, but was rescued by David. She bore David a son named Chileab.

versions.summary: Abigail is described as a woman of rare wisdom and beauty, married to the wealthy but foolish Nabal from the Carmel region in Judah. When Nabal insulted David by refusing his men during sheep shearing—a gross violation of the hospitality norms of that time—Abigail acted quickly and courageously. She gathered supplies, went to meet David, and delivered a remarkable speech marked by humility, wisdom, and prophetic insight, in which she among other things predicted that the Lord would establish a lasting dynasty for David. Her words convinced David to refrain from bloody revenge. After Nabal's sudden death, David took Abigail as his wife. She accompanied him during his time as a fugitive, was captured when the Amalekites raided Ziklag, but was rescued by David. She bore him a son named Chileab, who is also called Daniel.

footnotes.text: The name Abigail (Hebrew: אֲבִיגַיִל, Avigayil) likely means 'my father is joy' or 'source of joy'. This is a theophoric name that may suggest her father's joy was connected to God's blessing.

Shearing sheep (gez, גֵּז) was an important economic and social event in ancient Israel, often accompanied by celebration and hospitality. Wealthy sheep owners were expected to share their abundance with those who had protected their flocks. Nabal's rejection of David violated these deeply rooted norms of hospitality.

Abigail's speech to David in 1 Sam 25:24–31 is one of the longest and most well-crafted speeches by a woman in the Old Testament. Her words contain prophetic elements, including the promise of a 'lasting house' for David (v. 28), which seems to point forward to the Nathanic covenant in 2 Sam 7.

Kileab (כִּלְאָב), Abigail's son with David, is also called Daniel (דָּנִיֵּאל) in 1 Chr 3:1. He is mentioned as David's second son but plays no prominent role in the subsequent narrative, leading to speculation in rabbinic tradition that he died young.

Carmel (not to be confused with Mount Carmel in the north) was a town in the Judean highlands, near Maon, south of Hebron. Archaeological surveys have identified the site with Khirbet el-Kirmil, about 12 km southeast of Hebron, in an area suitable for sheep farming.

In rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Megilla 14a), Abigail is counted among the seven prophetesses of Israel. Her prophetic status is especially linked to her speech in 1 Sam 25, where she foretells David's royal future and speaks with divine insight.

The Hebrew word nabal (נָבָל) literally means 'fool' or 'simpleton'. Abigail herself plays on this etymology in 1 Sam 25:25 when she says: 'As his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly goes with him.' The symbolic function of the name underscores the literary contrast between Nabal's foolishness and Abigail's wisdom.
